summary: The narrator, facing the threat of the Lancer (a vicious murderer also hunting Martinez and Halliday), weighs letting himself be captured again so the DHS can take the Lancer down. The plan would require calling on Arthur for real help, which the narrator doubts Arthur would give, since the narrator has defied Arthur's requests and caused the mess. The passage is interior monologue ending with the narrator considering framing a deal for Arthur in terms of business, tied to protecting Halliday.
one_line: Fiction excerpt in which the narrator considers surrendering to the Lancer so the DHS can take him down, and doubts Arthur will help.
key_facts: The narrator's worst-case scenario is that the Lancer nabs them and then still goes after Martinez and Halliday without anyone being able to stop him.
The NSA had not been able to find the Lancer.
The narrator considers that they could make sure the DHS caught up with the Lancer, taking him by surprise.
Doing so would mean calling Arthur and asking him for help, not just for backup.
The narrator must let themselves get caught again instead of leading the Lancer on a chase.
The narrator fears the Lancer might take them out of the country and bury them somewhere outside U.S. jurisdiction.
If the Feds keep their protective detail on Halliday and Martinez drops off the map again, Arthur and the government task force would have no urgency in hunting the Lancer.
Halliday's voice in the narrator's head says: You don't trust him.
The narrator went after Martinez against Arthur's request, intending to lock her up until she gave over her proof.
The narrator used a man already known to be a vicious murderer to pursue Martinez.
The narrator reflects that their situation is cause and effect: play with matches and you'll get burned.
The narrator considers presenting a deal to Arthur as business that would make sense for him regarding Halliday.
